Reading @reason2026measuringcoherencepredictivemodels today made me realize
something surprising (but obvious in hindsight): Bayesian optimization (BO)
algorithms usually assume a predictive model which performs Bayesian updating,
even though approximate inference methods don't actually guarantee this. Let's
use a simple example with 2 variables, $y_1$ and $y_2$. A Bayesian model will
specify:

- $p_1(y_1)$: PDF[^pdf] of $y_1$
- $p_2(y_2)$: PDF of $y_2$
- $p_{12}(y_1, y_2)$: joint distribution of $y_1$ and $y_2$ together

[^pdf]: I'll just assume continuous $y$ to avoid needing to write PDF or PMF
    everywhere.

In a _coherent_ model, we have $p_1(y_1) = \int p_{12}(y_1, y_2)\, dy_2$ (and
vice versa for $p_2(y_2)$). This means we can freely choose between accessing
$p_1(y_1)$ directly or by marginalizing the joint distribution, whatever is
computationally more convenient. 

However, for many models in practical use $p_1(\cdot)$ and $\int p_{12}(\cdot,
y_2)\,dy_2$ may _not_ be equal. We call these models _incoherent_. Strictly
speaking, almost every model using approximate inference is likely to be
somewhat incoherent: eg inducing point GPs[^inducing-gps], prior-fitted
networks[^pfns], any probabilistic model sampled using MCMC[^mcmc].

[^inducing-gps]: If the inducing points are re-fit when conditioning on $y_2$
    (which is basically always done in practice) then it specifies a different
    model. I am aware of @maddox2021conditioning which proposes a different
    updating rule to avoid this, but haven't read this paper in detail.

[^pfns]: these are _amortized_ Bayesian methods, and the amortization might not
    be exact.

[^mcmc]: MCMC chains are finite in practice and may not fully mix, so
    re-running MCMC on the updated data won't exactly match the conditional
    implied by the original samples.

## Does coherence matter?

I suspect normally no, and I think this is why it's hardly mentioned in BO
papers. The vast majority of BO papers use acquisition functions that depend
only on marginals. For example, expected improvement, probability of
improvement, and upper confidence bound all just use $p(y)$. If a BO loop
chooses point 1 based on $p(y_1)$ and this causes an incoherent update to
$p(y_2)$ in the next step, that doesn't really matter too much, because these
are never directly compared.

However, some acquisition functions involve hypothetical model updates and
therefore _do_ implicitly assume coherence. For example, an
information-theoretic acquisition function like

$$
I(y_1, y_2) = H(y_2) - \mathbb E_{y_1} \left[ H(y_2 \mid y_1) \right]
$${#eq-mi}

implicitly relies on a coherent Bayesian update to produce $p(y_2 \mid y_1)$.
However, if this update is not made coherently, that doesn't actually guarantee
anything bad will happen. Maybe at worst this "pseudo mutual information" could
be negative.

@reason2026measuringcoherencepredictivemodels mainly points out that under
incoherent updating, different ways of writing an acquisition function may no
longer be equivalent. For example, mutual information can either be
a difference between unconditional and conditional entropies (like @eq-mi) or
a KL divergence between the joint and the product of marginals. These have
different analytic expressions and use different marginals/conditionals/joint
distributions and therefore might differ if the typical relationships between
these distributions don't hold.

## Importance for non-myopic BO

Non-myopic Bayesian optimization techniques (which include
information-theoretic ones) generally try to "look ahead" and reason about
future actions under a plausible set of labels for current proposed actions.
Clearly this assumes _some degree_ of coherence. I see two potential pitfalls.

### 1) Different updates between acquisition function and the outer loop

For example, when using inducing point GPs one might just add new proposed
actions as extra inducing points when calculating the acquisition function, but
do a full refit after acquiring new labels. This creates the potential for
a model to choose to observe point $x_1$ because of a scenario like "$y_1=7$
implies the optimum is $x_2$ with 99% probability", only for the model to have
a different estimate upon actually observing $y_1=7$. This kind of
inconsistency could make a model unable to properly follow through with its
plans.

### 2) Using an acquisition function with updates the model won't actually perform

Let's use entropy search [@hennig2012entropy] as an example. It assumes you
want to learn about the location of the maximizer $x^*$ of a function, and
proposes to use $I(x^*, y)$ as the acquisition function.

_Predictive_ entropy search [@hernandez2014predictive] proposes to re-write
this as:

$$
I(x^*, y) = H(y) - \mathbb E_{x^*} \left[ H(y \mid x^* ) \right] \ ,
$$

then goes on to propose an approximation for $p(y \mid x^*)$. Because of the
symmetry of mutual information,

$$
I(x^*, y) = H(y) - \mathbb E_{x^*} \left[ H(y \mid x^* ) \right] = H(x^*) - \mathbb E_{y} \left[ H(x^* \mid y ) \right] \ ,
$$

this expression _should_ therefore equal the model's entropy reduction about
$p(x^*)$. However, for an incoherent model this equality might not hold.
Because the model will never actually observe $x^*$, $p(y \mid x^*)$ represents
an update that the model will never actually perform. Instead, the model will
only perform an (approximate) update to $p(x^* \mid y)$, and this could be
completely inconsistent with what is calculated in the acquisition function.

## Conclusion

Overall this is nothing too new and nothing to be overly concerned about, but
if you are working on non-myopic BO my suggestion is to keep coherence in mind,
and try to use approximations that mirror the updates your model will actually
perform, instead of an idealized perfect update.
